Les tons (voir leurs notations en (1.4.3.)) aussi constituent des unités pertinentes et seront étudiés dans le chapitre suivant. — [2018, p. 15, §3.2.3 Les tons:] L'igo est une langue tonale. Elle utilise trois hauteurs mélodiques ou tons pour distinguer les mots. Les trois tons sont représentés comme suit : - Le ton Haut est représenté par un accent aigu sur la voyelle qui le porte ... - Le ton Bas est représenté par un accent grave sur la voyelle qui le porte ... - Le ton Moyen est marqué par l'absence de ton sur une voyelle

new_statements.translation: V = vowel without accent mark = vowel bearing Mid tone [...] V́ : vowel with acute accent = vowel bearing High tone / V̀ : vowel with grave accent = vowel bearing Low tone. The three tones can combine as a contour or a sequence of two or three tones on one vowel. (p. 28) — These meaningful units carry tones borne by the vowels. The tones (see their notation in 1.4.3) also constitute distinctive units and will be studied in the next chapter. (p. 32) — [2018, p. 15:] Igo is a tone language. It uses three pitch levels or tones to distinguish words.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Igo is described as a three-toneme language (High, Mid, Low, with contours on single vowels, downdrift and downstep); 'accent' in the sources means only the tone diacritics. No statement about word stress (placement, contrastiveness, or absence) occurs in any accessible page; the sections that could contain one (§2.5 La syllabe p. 62, §2.6 Le mot phonologique p. 77, Ch. 3 Le système tonal pp. 99-142) are outside the free preview.
new_statements.exceptions: None (no stress rule given). Vowel length is stated to be non-phonemic (p. 29).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone description (nouns = class prefix + mostly monosyllabic CV radical, p. 31); tonal perturbations described at noun-phrase and verb-phrase level (TOC pp. 135-142, 342-364).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the igo (Ahlon/Ahlo/Bogo) of the Bogo canton, Danyi prefecture, Plateaux Region, south-west Togo (5 villages, ~7,000 speakers, one dependent farm in Ghana) — the same variety as Glottolog igoo1238; no dialect split is mentioned. 'Ahlo' in Westermann 1922 / Heine 1968 is the German-era name for the same language.

new_statements.quote: [p. 7, Tonhöhen, §4] Der musikalische Ton tritt ebenso deutlich hervor und ist von derselben Bedeutung wie im Ewe. Die Präfixe haben ihre eigenen Töne; ihr Ton hat sich also nicht wie in anderen Sprachen dem des Wortstammes angeglichen oder einfach Tiefton angenommen. [§5] Wörter, die bei gleichem Lautbestand nur durch verschiedene Töne sich unterscheiden, sind häufig [...] Beispiele: òdo Berg, ódò Ortschaft; àfa Bohne, afá Leber [...] — [p. 18, §28] Die häufigste Verneinungspartikel ist na; sie unterscheidet sich von dem na des Futurums und des Habitualis durch einen außerordentlich hohen Ton und einen dynamischen Akzent. — [p. 19] Der Habitualis wird verneint mittels hochtonigem und stark betontem tá [...]
new_statements.translation: [p. 7 §4] Musical tone stands out just as clearly and has the same significance as in Ewe. The prefixes have their own tones; their tone has thus not, as in other languages, assimilated to that of the word stem or simply taken low tone. [§5] Words that with the same segments are distinguished only by different tones are frequent [...] Examples: òdo 'mountain', ódò 'village'; àfa 'bean', afá 'liver' [...] — [p. 18 §28] The commonest negative particle is na; it differs from the na of the future and of the habitual by an extraordinarily high tone and a dynamic (stress) accent. — [p. 19] The habitual is negated by means of high-toned and strongly stressed tá [...]
new_statements.citation: Westermann, D. 1922. Die Sprache der Guang in Togo und auf der Goldküste und fünf andere Togosprachen. Berlin: Reimer. (Ahlo section)

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog record (tonal; Gblem-Poidi 2021: three level tones H/M/L, no stress statement). Westermann 1922 likewise treats Ahlo as tonal (Hochton/Tiefton/Mittelton, minimal pairs) and gives no word-stress rule; the one added detail is that the negative particles ná/tá bear an extra-high tone with dynamic stress (pp. 18-19), a particle-level emphasis remark, not a word-stress placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Westermann describes Ahlo (Igo) as a tone language like Ewe: lexically distinctive musical tone (high, low, mid, plus contour tones per the Vorwort notation pp. 2-3), prefixes with their own tones, many tonal minimal pairs, tone also active in verb conjugation (§6). There is no section on word stress/accent and no statement of where stress falls or whether it exists as a word-level property; the only accent remarks are morpheme-specific: the negative particle ná carries an extra-high tone and a 'dynamic accent' (§28, p. 18), and the negative-habitual tá is 'high-toned and strongly stressed' (p. 19).
new_statements.exceptions: none (only the emphatic prominence of the negative particles ná and tá, pp. 18-19)
new_statements.identity_note: Westermann's 'Ahlo' (self-name Agō, people Bogo, sg. Ogoebi; Ewe exonym Ahlõ) is Igo/Ahlon, igoo1238; data recorded in Lome in 1907 from several Ahlo speakers (p. 6). the copy we hold sits in the baat1238 (Bargu/Baatonum) folder because the same volume treats six languages; igoo1238/ carries the pointer.

sources.note: Only the publisher's free preview (pp. 1-40 and 474-484) could be downloaded. Sommaire (p. 9) shows Ch. 2 Système phonologique (2.5 La syllabe p. 62; 2.6 Le mot phonologique p. 77) and Ch. 3 Le système tonal (pp. 99-142, three tonemes H/M/B, schèmes tonals, downdrift, downstep). In the readable pages 'accent' is used only for the tone diacritics (p. 28: acute = ton Haut, grave = ton Bas, unmarked = ton Moyen; three tones can combine on one vowel); p. 29: no phonological vowel length; p. 32: tones are borne by vowels and are distinctive units. No sentence on word stress in the accessible pages…
